plan: Informative essay (CLD-P-ACT-E-000058) on Maria Mitchell: her 1847 comet discovery from a Nantucket rooftop, the King of Denmark's medal, election to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, teaching at Vassar from 1865, the 1878 Denver eclipse trip, and her demand for equal pay. Topic checked against every bank and the combined bank (no matches). Ten new items with two NO CHANGE keys. Plus E057-06 resubmitted as revision 2 on banked passage CLD-P-ACT-E-000057 (trap label only). Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Miss Mitchell's Comet
passages.text:
[1] On an October night in 1847, Maria Mitchell climbed to the roof of her family's home on Nantucket, Massachusetts, {{1|and, swept}} the sky with a small telescope. [2] Near the North Star she noticed a faint, fuzzy patch of light that had not been there {{2|before: a comet}} that no one had yet reported.

[3] {{3|Having discovered the comet, a gold medal was awarded to Mitchell}} by the King of Denmark, under a standing royal offer of a medal to the first person to find each new comet through a telescope. [4] The next year, she became the first woman elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. {{4|}}

[5] In 1865, Mitchell joined the faculty of Vassar College, a new school for women, {{5|where}} she taught astronomy for more than twenty years. [6] She believed that students learned best by observing the sky for themselves rather than {{6|to read}} about it. [7] In 1878, she {{7|lead}} a group of students to Denver, Colorado, to observe a total eclipse of the Sun.

[8] Mitchell also fought for fair treatment. [9] {{8|However,}} when she learned that younger male professors earned more than she did, she {{9|demanded—and received, a raise}}.

passages.title: Death in a Nutshell
passages.text:
[1] Frances Glessner Lee was born in 1878 into a wealthy Chicago family that expected her to marry, run a household, and stay out of {{1|public life, she did}} all three for many years. [2] A friendship in middle age changed her course.

[3] Through her brother, Lee met George Burgess Magrath, a medical examiner {{2|whom}} described how often deaths were misjudged by investigators with no medical training. [4] Lee became convinced that careful observation could be taught, and in 1931 she helped fund a department of legal medicine at Harvard.

[5] In the 1940s, Lee {{3|begins}} building a series of miniature rooms. [6] Each one, built at a scale of one inch to one foot, {{4|recreate}} a death scene, drawn from real cases, in painstaking detail. [7] The rooms contained windows that opened, calendars set to the right date, and {{5|tiny cans of food with readable labels}}.

[8] Lee called the dioramas the "Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death." [9] Police officers attending her week-long seminars at Harvard {{6|carefully and meticulously studied them}}. [10] The officers were not expected to solve the cases. [11] {{7|Instead,}} they were asked to observe and describe what they saw, so that they would learn not to jump to conclusions.

[12] Most of the dioramas survive today at the medical examiner's office in {{8|Baltimore, Maryland where}} they are still used to train investigators.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: climbed to the roof of her family's home
candidates.explanation: "Climbed" and "swept" share the subject "Maria Mitchell," so no comma is needed between "and" and "swept."

A.rationale: A comma should not separate "and" from the verb it joins to the sentence.

C.rationale: The comma wrongly separates the subject "she" from its verb.

D.rationale: A semicolon cannot join a verb phrase to the rest of the sentence.

strategy.explanation: Find the subject of each verb.

candidates.remember: Do not use a comma to split a compound predicate after "and."

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: Near the North Star she noticed a faint, fuzzy patch of light
candidates.explanation: A colon can introduce a phrase that identifies what came before; "a comet that no one had yet reported" explains what the patch of light was.

B.rationale: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and "a comet that no one had yet reported" is not one.

C.rationale: This leaves "A comet that no one had yet reported" as a sentence fragment.

D.rationale: Without punctuation, the sentence seems to say the light was there before a comet.

hints: Is the part after the punctuation a full sentence?

strategy.explanation: Test each choice for fragments and clause rules.

candidates.remember: A colon can introduce an explanation after a complete clause.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: Having discovered the comet, Mitchell's gold medal was awarded
choices.C: Having discovered the comet, Mitchell was awarded a gold medal
choices.D: Having discovered the comet, the medal went to Mitchell

candidates.explanation: The person who discovered the comet was Mitchell, so "Mitchell" must come right after the opening phrase.

A.rationale: The opening phrase seems to say that the gold medal discovered the comet.

B.rationale: The opening phrase now modifies "gold medal," not Mitchell.

D.rationale: The opening phrase now modifies "the medal," not Mitchell.

strategy.explanation: Put the doer right after the introductory phrase.

candidates.remember: An introductory modifier must describe the word right after the comma.

candidates.stem:
At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence:
Nantucket is an island about thirty miles south of Cape Cod.
Should the writer make this addition here?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains why Mitchell received a medal from the King of Denmark.
choices.B: Yes, because it tells where Mitchell was elected to the American Academy.
choices.C: No, because it contradicts the claim that Mitchell lived in Massachusetts.
choices.D: No, because it interrupts her list of honors with a geographic detail.

candidates.evidence: she became the first woman elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences
candidates.explanation: The paragraph lists honors Mitchell received for her discovery; a fact about Nantucket's location distracts from that focus.

A.rationale: Geography does not explain the medal.

B.rationale: The sentence is about Nantucket's location, not about where she was elected.

C.rationale: Nantucket is part of Massachusetts, so there is no contradiction.

strategy.explanation: Compare the sentence with the paragraph's focus.

candidates.remember: Add a sentence only if it supports the paragraph's point.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: Vassar College, a new school for women
candidates.explanation: The clause describes a place, Vassar College, so "where" correctly introduces it.

B.rationale: "Which she taught astronomy" leaves the clause without a logical link to the college.

C.rationale: "When" refers to a time, but the clause describes a place.

D.rationale: "In that" means "because," which does not fit the meaning.

hints: Does the clause describe a place, a time, or a thing?

strategy.explanation: Substitute each choice and read the sentence.

candidates.remember: Use "where" to introduce a clause about a place.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: students learned best by observing the sky for themselves
candidates.explanation: "Rather than" compares two things that should have the same form: "observing" and "reading."

A.rationale: "By observing ... rather than to read" mixes a gerund with an infinitive.

C.rationale: "They read" adds a clause that breaks the parallel with "observing."

D.rationale: "Having read" shifts the time and breaks the parallel.

hints: What form is the word paired with this one?
candidates.remember: Items joined by "rather than" should be parallel.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: The past tense of "lead" is "led," which fits an event in 1878.

A.rationale: "Lead" is the present tense; the sentence describes 1878.

B.rationale: "Leaded" is not the past tense of "lead."

C.rationale: The present perfect does not fit an event fixed in 1878.

hints: What is the past tense of "lead"?

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: Mitchell also fought for fair treatment
candidates.explanation: Sentence 9 gives an example of the fair treatment she fought for, so "For instance" fits.

A.rationale: Demanding a raise does not contrast with fighting for fair treatment; it is an example of it.

B.rationale: Her demand was not a replacement for fighting for fair treatment.

D.rationale: Fighting for fair treatment did not cause her to learn about the pay gap.

hints: How does sentence 9 relate to sentence 8?
candidates.remember: Use "For instance" when a sentence illustrates the one before it.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: when she learned that younger male professors earned more
candidates.explanation: "And received" interrupts "demanded ... a raise" and must be set off with matching marks on both sides.

A.rationale: An interruption opened with a dash must close with a dash, not a comma.

B.rationale: The interruption opens with a comma but closes with a dash.

C.rationale: The interruption opens with a dash but is never closed.

hints: Where does the interruption begin and end?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence without the interruption.

candidates.remember: Set off an interruption with matching punctuation on both sides.

candidates.subskill: Evaluating whether an essay meets a goal
candidates.stem: Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to explain the methods astronomers use to discover comets. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?

choices.A: Yes, because it describes Mitchell sweeping the sky with a telescope.
choices.B: No, because it traces Mitchell's career rather than explaining methods.
choices.C: Yes, because it explains why the King of Denmark offered a medal.
choices.D: No, because it never mentions that Mitchell discovered a comet.

candidates.evidence: she became the first woman elected
candidates.explanation: The essay covers Mitchell's discovery, honors, teaching and fight for fair pay; it does not explain how comets are discovered.

A.rationale: One sentence about her observing does not explain astronomers' methods.

C.rationale: The essay mentions the medal but does not explain discovery methods.

D.rationale: The essay says she discovered a comet.

hints: What does most of the essay discuss?

strategy.explanation: Check the essay against the exact purpose.

candidates.remember: Judge the whole essay against the goal.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: studied them closely and with care
choices.D: closely studied them in a careful way

candidates.evidence: Police officers attending her week-long seminars
candidates.explanation: "Studied them closely" expresses the idea once, without repetition.

A.rationale: "Carefully" and "meticulously" mean nearly the same thing, so using both is redundant.

B.rationale: "Closely" and "with care" repeat the same idea.

D.rationale: "Closely" and "in a careful way" repeat the same idea.

hints: Do any words say the same thing twice?

strategy.explanation: Pick the most concise choice that keeps the meaning.

candidates.remember: Avoid words that repeat an idea.
